'''Arnold Schönhage''' (born 1 December 1934 in [[Lockhausen]], now [[Bad Salzuflen]]) is a German [[mathematician]] and [[computer scientist]].

Schönhage was professor at the [[University of Bonn|Rheinische Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universität, Bonn]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Luerweg |first=Frank |date=December 21, 2004 |title=Weltrekord-Rechenmethode kommt zu späten Ehren |url=https://idw-online.de/de/news95114 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=Informationsdienst Wissenschaft}}</ref> and also in [[Tübingen]] and [[Konstanz]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arnold Schönhage |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=24765 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=The Mathematics Genealogy Project |publisher=North Dakota State University}}</ref>

Together with [[Volker Strassen]], he developed the [[Schönhage–Strassen algorithm]] for the multiplication of large numbers<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Fischer |first=Lars |date=April 11, 2019 |title=Mathematik: Die schnellste Art zu multiplizieren |url=https://www.spektrum.de/news/die-schnellste-art-zu-multiplizieren/1638472 |access-date=2023-10-21 |website=Spektrum der Wissenschaft |language=de}}</ref> that has a [[Runtime (program lifecycle phase)|runtime]] of ''[[Big O notation|O]]''(''N''&nbsp;log&nbsp;''N''&nbsp;log&nbsp;log&nbsp;''N''). For many years, this was the fastest known way to multiply large integers, although Schönhage and Strassen predicted that an algorithm with a run-time of N(logN) should exist. In 2019, [[Joris van der Hoeven]] and David Harvey finally developed an algorithm with this runtime, proving that Schönhage's and Strassen's prediction had been correct.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Klarreich |first=Erica |authorlink=Erica Klarreich|date=2019-12-20 |title=Multiplication hits the speed limit |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3371387 |journal=Communications of the ACM |language=en |volume=63 |issue=1 |pages=11–13 |doi=10.1145/3371387 |s2cid=209450552 |issn=0001-0782|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Schönhage designed and implemented together with [[Andreas F. W. Grotefeld]] and [[Ekkehart Vetter]] a multitape [[Turing machine]], called [[Turing processor|TP]], in software. The machine is programmed in [[TPAL]], an [[assembler language]]. They implemented numerous numerical algorithms, including the Schönhage–Strassen algorithm, on this machine.

The [[Odlyzko–Schönhage algorithm]]<ref name="Odlyzko Schonhage 1988">{{cite journal | last=Odlyzko | first=A. M. | author1-link=Andrew Odlyzko | last2=Schönhage | first2=A. | title=Fast Algorithms for Multiple Evaluations of the Riemann Zeta Function | journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society | volume=309 | issue=2 | date=1988 | doi=10.2307/2000939 | pages=797-809}}</ref> from 1988 is regularly used in research on the [[Riemann zeta function]].
